links.note: Pope Innocent III approved the Humiliati around 1200, and many later popes confirmed them. The order then grew fast. In the province of Milan alone it soon had more than two hundred houses.

prose_changes.old: Sibling-rival of the Dominicans; parent of Observants and Spirituals; its lay third order (Order of Penance, 1221) rides inside its own story
prose_changes.new: Sibling and rival of the Dominicans. Parent of the Spirituals, and through its later order of the Observants. Its lay third order, the Order of Penance of 1221, belongs inside its own story.
prose_changes.reason: The Observance began in 1368, inside the order as it ran on after 1300, which is a separate movement on the tree; the new wording says the parentage runs through it. The Spirituals arose before 1300 (Celestine V's grant of 1294) and are linked directly. Split into sentences for reading level; every fact kept.

prose_changes.old: Lay penitential wool-workers condemned alongside the Waldensians and then re-absorbed - the mirror image of the Waldensians themselves: the same 1184 condemnation, the opposite outcome.
prose_changes.new: Lay wool-workers who lived a life of penance. Later writers say they were condemned with the Waldensians in 1184, and then taken back into the church. If so, they are the Waldensians' mirror image: the same condemnation, the opposite outcome.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored or repo-cited text shows the 1184 decree naming the Humiliati. The only vendored witness is Foxe's sixteenth-century report of a chronicler (Acts and Monuments vol. 4, lines 38608-38611), and the census's own Catholic Encyclopedia source does not mention the condemnation. The claim is kept, said to rest on report. Rewritten whole for reading level.

prose_changes.old: In twelfth-century Lombardy, groups of lay wool-workers and weavers began living out a simple, demanding vision of penitence — plain dress, manual labor, and a rejection of the oath-taking and violence expected of feudal society. And called themselves the Humiliati, 'the humbled ones.' In 1184 they were condemned alongside the Waldensians for preaching without official permission, but where the Waldensians' story became one of lasting separation, theirs took the opposite turn. Pope Innocent III reconciled them in 1201, organizing them into three recognized orders. Two religious, one for married lay people who stayed in ordinary working life under a shared rule. For roughly two centuries afterward they remained a real presence in northern Italian towns, their rule and community records still surviving, until the movement was formally suppressed by papal bull in 1571.
prose_changes.new: In twelfth-century Lombardy, groups of lay wool-workers and weavers began to live a simple, demanding life of penance. They wore plain dress and worked with their hands. They refused the oaths and the violence that feudal society expected. They called themselves the Humiliati, 'the humbled ones.' In 1184 Pope Lucius III condemned the Waldensians for preaching without leave. Later writers say he condemned the Humiliati with them. If so, their story then took the opposite turn. The Waldensians stayed apart for good, but Pope Innocent III took the Humiliati back in 1201. He made them three recognized orders. Two were religious orders. The third was for married lay people who stayed in ordinary working life under a shared rule. For about two centuries they were a real presence in the towns of northern Italy. Their rule and community records still survive. In 1571 a papal bull shut down the order of Humiliati brothers.
prose_changes.reason: Two relationship claims corrected. The 1184 decree against the Waldensians is supported (Montet 1885, lines 2249-2250); its naming of the Humiliati rests on Foxe's late report. The 1571 bull abolished the order of brothers ('Ordinem Fratrum Humiliatorum', Bullarium Romanum 2, lines 92832-92835), and the Catholic Encyclopedia says the women's houses were not affected, so 'the movement was formally suppressed' was too broad. 'Two centuries ... until 1571' also read as 370 years of presence; now two sentences. The fragment 'And called themselves...' is joined back. Rewritten whole for reading level, with plainer words where they keep the sense ('penance' for 'penitence', 'without leave' for 'without official permission', 'took them back' for 'reconciled them', 'shut down' for 'suppressed'); every other fact kept.

prose_changes.old: In twelfth-century Lombardy, lay wool-workers and weavers took up plain dress, manual labor and a rejection of the oath-taking and violence expected of feudal society, calling themselves the Humiliati, 'the humbled ones.' Condemned alongside the Waldensians in 1184 for preaching without permission, they took the opposite path: Pope Innocent III reconciled them in 1201, organizing them into three orders, two religious and one for married lay people who stayed in ordinary working life. They refused the oaths and violence that feudal society expected, and called themselves the Humiliati, 'the humbled ones.' Later writers say they were condemned with the Waldensians in 1184 for preaching without leave. If so, they then took the opposite path. Pope Innocent III took them back in 1201 and made them three orders. Two were religious. The third was for married lay people who stayed in ordinary working life. They were a real presence in the towns of northern Italy for about two centuries. In 1571 a papal bull shut down the order of Humiliati brothers.
prose_changes.reason: The same two corrections as the long description: the 1184 naming rests on report, and the 1571 bull abolished the brothers' order, not the whole movement. Rewritten whole for reading level; every other fact kept.

prose_changes.old: No clear record survives of lasting influence beyond their own two centuries — when the order was suppressed by papal bull in 1571, its distinct identity ended with it.
prose_changes.new: No clear record survives of their lasting influence beyond their own two centuries. In 1571 a papal bull shut down the brothers' order, and with it the movement mostly lost its own identity. Some houses of Humiliati nuns lived on.
prose_changes.reason: The Catholic Encyclopedia (the census's own source, read 2026-11-07) says the women's congregation was not affected by the 1571 bull and that five houses remained in Italy when it wrote. 'Its distinct identity ended with it' was too strong.

prose_changes.old: From the late twelfth century, women in the towns of the Low Countries and the Rhineland began living religious lives without joining any order: no lifelong vows, no rule, no enclosure. They kept their own property or worked — often in cloth — lived alone or in walled courtyard communities called beguinages, prayed, and nursed the sick and the dying. Some of them wrote, and that is what makes them extraordinary on any map of medieval Christianity: Hadewijch's visions and letters, Mechthild of Magdeburg's Flowing Light of the Godhead, Marguerite Porete's Mirror of Simple Souls are among the very few medieval accounts of a religious life told from the inside by the women actually living it. Because they fitted no category, they attracted suspicion: Porete was burned in Paris in 1310, and in 1312 the Council of Vienne moved against the beguine life itself.
prose_changes.new: From the late twelfth century, women in the towns of the Low Countries and the Rhineland began to live religious lives without joining any order. They took no lifelong vows, kept no rule and lived under no enclosure. They kept their own property or worked, often in cloth. Some lived alone, others in walled courtyard communities called beguinages. They prayed, and nursed the sick and the dying. Some of them wrote, and that is what makes them extraordinary on any map of medieval Christianity. Hadewijch wrote visions and letters. Mechthild of Magdeburg wrote The Flowing Light of the Godhead, and Marguerite Porete wrote The Mirror of Simple Souls. These are among the very few medieval accounts of a religious life told from the inside, by the women living it. Because they fitted no category, they drew suspicion. Porete was burned in Paris in 1310. In 1312 the Council of Vienne condemned errors it laid on beguines and beghards.
prose_changes.reason: The vendored evidence (Denzinger 471, lines 14792-14793; Antoninus in Mansi 25, lines 39817-39819) shows the council condemning errors it attributed to beguines and beghards. The decree against the beguine status itself (Cum de quibusdam mulieribus) is not vendored or repo-cited; it is in the wants list, and with it the sentence can again say the council moved against the beguine life itself. Rewritten whole for reading level; every other fact kept.

prose_changes.old: The decree Ad nostrum, issued at the Council of Vienne in 1312, listed eight errors said to be held by a 'sect of the Free Spirit'. Chiefly that a soul perfected in this life becomes incapable of sin and needs neither the church nor the virtues any longer.
prose_changes.new: The decree Ad nostrum, issued at the Council of Vienne in 1312, listed eight errors said to be held by beguines and beghards in Germany. Their core claim was that a soul made perfect in this life can no longer sin, and needs neither the church nor the virtues any longer. One error spoke of people living 'in the spirit of liberty'.
prose_changes.reason: The vendored text of the eight errors (Denzinger 471-478) heads them 'Errores Beguardorum et Beguinarum', and Antoninus of Florence places them 'in Alemannia' (Mansi 25, lines 39817-39819). No vendored text has the decree calling them a 'sect of the Free Spirit'; the quotation marks presented a later label as the decree's words. The third error's 'spiritu libertatis' (Denzinger 473, line 14808) is now quoted instead. The fragment 'Chiefly that...' is made a sentence.

prose_changes.old: In 1312 the Council of Vienne's decree Ad nostrum listed eight errors said to belong to a 'sect of the Free Spirit,' chiefly that a soul perfected in this life needs neither the church nor the virtues any longer — and interrogators then went looking for people who held them, finding them because the questions supplied the answers. Robert Lerner's 1972 study concluded that no organized sect of this kind ever existed; what existed was a wide spectrum of mystical piety, much of it among beguines and beghards, and a charge that could be laid against any part of it. Marguerite Porete's own book, once separated from the label, has since been read as a serious work of theology.
prose_changes.new: In 1312 the Council of Vienne's decree Ad nostrum listed eight errors said to belong to beguines and beghards in Germany. Their core claim was that a soul made perfect in this life needs neither the church nor the virtues any longer. Interrogators then went looking for people who held them. They found them, because the questions supplied the answers. Robert Lerner's 1972 study concluded that no organized sect of this kind ever existed. What existed was a wide spectrum of mystical piety, much of it among beguines and beghards, and a charge that could be laid against any part of it. Marguerite Porete's own book, once separated from the label, has since been read as a serious work of theology.
prose_changes.reason: As in the long description. Rewritten whole for reading level; every other fact kept.
